questions.help:
Road traffic collisions      
     
2 Road traffic collisions can be avoided  
2.2 Factors involved in collisions
Generally, the factors that influence the occurrence of a traffic collision are varied, but always one or more of these factors are involved: the vehicle, the road (& environment) and the driver.
Not all risk factors are equally important. Of every 100 collisions, only between 4 and 13 are due mainly to vehicle factors (for example, a defective tyre or deficient brakes) and only between 10 and 35 are due mainly to the road and related environment factors (for example, when the roadway is wet and the vehicle loses control).
Most collisions, between 70 and 90%, are due to the human factor (for example, the driver becomes distracted, or speeds or is under the influence of alcohol etc).
(Página 249 del manual 'Learning to drive')

6. Groups of drivers most at risk of a collision    
6.2 The elderly
Older people who have suffered a deterioration of psychomotor skills that are important for driving (such as a reduced ability to concentrate or an increase in the time it takes to react) may have more collisions in complex situations that require quick response, especially at junctions and at the entries and exits of roads when driving at high speed.
Conversely, in situations when there is enough time to react, they have the same problems as other younger people. Due to this, you must give the elderly enough time and not put pressure on them.

Does speed influence reaction time?
questions.help:
Physical condition of the driver    
 
4 Reaction time
The reaction time can be increased by:
fatigue or tiredness,
drowsiness, sleepiness,
the advancement of age,
the loss of vision and poor hearing,
poor state of health,
the use of medications,
the intake of alcohol, drugs or other narcotics substances,
heavy and excessive meals,
the excessive heat in the cockpit of the vehicle,
the emotional state.
the attention level of the driver.
All these listed factors have the serious potential consequence of reducing the driver’s ability to react and therefore the result is an increase in the reaction time.
(Página 32 del manual 'Learning to drive')

12 Distances
 
12.1 The reaction distance
The reaction distance is the distance travelled by the vehicle from the time of seeing a hazard until he reacts to it.
It is dependant on the speed and the driver’s reaction time, which in turn depends, on many other factors, such as, the driver’s reflexes, their psycho-physical state (level of alertness, whether or not the driver is under the influence of alcohol etc.) Even the environment can affect the time it takes for a driver to react to any given circumstance (the passenger compartment temperature, noise, etc.)
A reaction time of 0.75 seconds is considered to be normal, during which time the vehicle will travel a distance, determined by the speed at which the vehicle is travelling.
(Página 179 del manual 'Learning to drive')

3.2 Beaconing elements
3.2.2 Guiding devices
3.2.2.10 Longitudinal auditory guides
Small grooves in the pavement or raised markings that, when driven over, produce vibration and/or sound. Their purpose is to alert drivers to unintended deviations from the vehicle’s trajectory.

11 Crash helmets
 
11.1 Tips for buying a crash helmet
Visors:
Visors are strongly recommended. However, it is important to ensure that these do not mist up; therefore, special covers are available that increase the anti-mist properties. When the helmet does not include eye protection it is highly recommended that safety glasses are used, although this use is not mandatory. Without eye protection, there is obviously the risk that something may enter the eye (an insect, a particle of sand or dust, etc.,) which may cause the rider to become distracted; however, the cold and/or the wind constantly in the eyes also increases visual fatigue.
(Página 82 del manual 'Learning to drive')

questions.question:
A partir de la señal de la fotografía, ¿qué distancia de seguridad es obligatorio mantener, como mínimo, con la motocicleta?
From the sign in the photograph, what is the minimum safety distance required to be maintained from the motorbike?
questions.help:
12 Distances
 
12.5 Safety distance
Any driver of a vehicle driving behind another must leave space that allows them to stop without colliding in the event of sudden braking, taking into account, in particular, speed, grip and braking conditions. However, a group of cyclists does not need to keep this distance, paying close attention to avoid collisions.
When it is possible for vehicles behind you to overtake, then in addition to leaving a sufficient separation distance so that in case of sudden braking by the vehicle ahead of you – you don’t crash into the back of it, you should additionally leave a gap to allow overtaking vehicles to overtake safely. (Note: that his rule is not applicable to a group of cyclists travelling together.)
Vehicles with a MAM greater than 3500 kgs, vehicles and combinations / sets of vehicles over 10m long, must keep a minimum safety distance of 50 m.
(Página 180 del manual 'Learning to drive')

12 Distances
 
12.5 Safety distance
The obligation to leave a safety distance where it is possible for the vehicle behind to overtake is not applicable to the following circumstances:
In a built-up-area (within town and cities etc.).
Where overtaking is forbidden.
Where there is more than 1 lane for the direction travelled.
When intense traffic does not permit overtaking.
(Página 180 del manual 'Learning to drive')
